Kaṇṇappa
------------------------------------------
Hindu didactic literature, especially of the mythological type, has tried to convince the masses that God is more pleased with the pure devotion of a simple heart than with the ostentatious devotion of rituals and allied paraphernalia.
Kaṇṇappa (also known as Beḍara कण्णप्प, the head of the hunters’ tribe) is one of the 63 Śaiva saints—the tenth among them—pictured in such works.
His story is given in the Tamil Periyapurāṇam (of Sekkilar, 11th century A. D.) as also in certain Kannada literary works like Vṛṣabhendravijaya of Ṣaḍakṣari (17th century A. D.) and the Ragaḷes of हरिहर (13th century A. D.).
Kaṇṇappa was the chief of the hunters living at the foot of the hills near Kāḷahasti (now in Andhra Pradesh). Once शिव appeared in his dream and asked him to worship the शिवलिङ्ग in the nearby forest. कण्णप्प soon discovered the शिवलिङ्ग he had seen in the dream in a nearby desolate temple and started worshipping it in most unorthodox and even abominable ways with meat and flowers worn by him on his own body! The ब्राह्मण priest doing regular worship used to find the लिङ्ग ‘desecrated’ every day!
One day when he was hiding in the temple to catch the culprit, he found कण्णप्प entering. Just at that time, blood started oozing from the eye of Lord शिव’s लिङ्ग. कण्णप्प plucked one of his eyes and fixed it on the लिङ्ग. Then the second eye on the लिङ्ग also started bleeding. When कण्णप्प was about to pluck his other eye also, the Lord appeared there and blessed him.
Kaṇṇappa got back his eyes and also enjoyed the bliss of seeing शिव and adoring him. The ब्राह्मण priest, realising the greatness of this devotee, fell at his feet.

kaṇṭakaśodhana
(‘searching [and punishing] evil persons’)
------------------------------------------
Running a kingdom is a challenging task. A king has to look at the management side not only from the positive angle, but also from the negative angle. ‘Kaṇṭaka-śodhana’ belongs to this latter group.
‘Kaṇṭaka’ literally means a ‘thorn’ and figuratively, a ‘harmful person’. A ruler has to organise a set of good spies who can not only find out but also catch red-handed, the culprits who are against the people and against the nation. Such an act was known as ‘kaṇṭakaśodhana’ (vide section 4 of the Arthaśāstra of कौटिल्य [300 B. C.]).
Some of the items listed under ‘kaṇṭakaśodhana’ by the Arthaśāstra are:
Whether the artisans working in the guilds were maintaining the quality of the work and giving the finished articles on time; whether the weights and measures used by the traders were genuine and standard; whether the traders, workers and manufacturers were maintaining the standards set for them and selling unadulterated things; whether the government officers were taking bribes or cheating the State; whether the doctors were treating their patients as per the एथिच्स् of medical science and so on.
The espionage system described and prescribed by कौटिल्य was quite elaborate and almost fool-proof.
See also ARTHAŚĀSTRA.

Kaṇṇagi
------------------------------------------
Kaṇṇagi was a lady of ideal wifely virtues who was later deified in Tamil history. See ŚILAPPADIKĀRAM for details.

Kāṇvaśākhā
------------------------------------------
The Śukla Yajurveda has two शाखास् or recensions; the Kāṇvaśākhā and the Mādhyandinaśākhā.
The Śatapatha Brāhmaṇa also has two शाखास् of the same name. The Bṛhadā-raṇyaka Upaniṣad is found in both the recensions. The Kāṇvaśākhā has 17 kāṇḍas or chapters and the Mādhyandina-śākhā 14.
There is not much difference between these two recensions.
See also BṚHADĀRAṆYAKA UPANIṢAD.

kāṇḍarṣi
(‘the sage of the kāṇḍa [or section of the वेदस्]’)
------------------------------------------
The वेदस् are generally divided into two kāṇḍas or sections: the कर्मकाण्ड and the ज्ञानकाण्ड dealing with Vedic rituals and knowledge respectively. The chief ṛṣis or sages who have expounded these are called ‘kāṇḍarṣis’.
The former was expounded by जैमिनि and the latter by बादरायण व्यास. So, these two are specifically known as ‘kāṇḍarṣis’.
Sometimes, the sage शाण्डिल्य is recognised as the third काण्डर्षि since he expounded the भक्ति aspect of the वेदस् as different from the कर्म and the ज्ञान aspects. He calls the ज्ञानकाण्ड section as Brahmakāṇḍa.

Kaṇāda
------------------------------------------
Vaiśeṣika-दर्शन, one of the six systems of Hindu philosophy grouped under the आस्तिक schools—schools that accept the authority of the Vedas—owes its systematisation to the sage कणाद, who was also known as Aulūkya. He was probably living by the उञ्छवृत्ति or subsisting on small grains and hence got the name कणाद (kaṇa = small grain, ad = to eat). Since he was the son of the sage Ulūka, he was called Aulūkya (son of, or, belonging to the family of, Ulūka). Nothing is known about him. According to some scholars he might have lived before बुद्ध and belonged to प्रभास in Saurāṣṭra (Gujarat).
See VAIŚEṢIKA DARŚANA also.

Kaṇva
------------------------------------------
‘Kaṇva’ seems to be the name of many sages. In the Ṛgveda, one कण्व, son of Ghora, has been mentioned as the author of 101 ṛks or Ṛgvedic mantras.
A more famous कण्व is the sage who was the foster-ड़थेर् of शकुन्तला. He not only brought her up but also took her to the king दुष्यन्त, her husband. He was the son of another well-known sage मेधातिथि.
He once advised दुर्योधन to make peace with the Pāṇḍavas. But, the prince refused to listen and patted his thighs in arrogance. Then कण्व cursed him that he would die with broken thighs.
His hermitage has been traced to a place near the modern Lucknow (in Uttar Pradesh).
